newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. sends envoy Ross to Mideast to tackle crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sends envoy Ross to Mideast to tackle crisis.

text.p: The United States ordered its chief Middle East peace broker back to the region on Wednesday for what President Bill Clinton said would be an attempt to stop Israeli-Palestinian violence and restart peace talks.

Clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops flared for a seventh straight day, this time in self-ruled Ramallah in the West Bank where hundreds of Arabs threw stones and bottles to challenge soldiers at a checkpoint.
Troops responded with rubber bullets and teargas. A Ramallah hospital said about 25 protesters were treated either for rubber bullet wounds or teargas inhalation.

Clinton told reporters in Washington he was sending envoy Dennis Ross to meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in Rabat, Morocco and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem because he was concerned about the peace process.

"We have been talking among ourselves here intensely over the last several days about whether there are some ideas we ought to advance with the Israelis and the Palestinians, and particularly what we can do to minimise the violence and to get the negotiations back going," Clinton said.

The crisis erupted when Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement of 6,500 houses last week in Arab East Jerusalem. Clashes broke out a week ago and on Friday, a Palestinian suicide bomber killed three Israeli women at a Tel Aviv cafe.

"They (the Palestinian Authority) have clearly shown the...physical and political ability to control this terrorism but they have chosen in recent days to use terrorism as a weapon of negotiations," Netanyahu said in speech in central Israel.

"We expect and we would like to see the Palestinian Authority fight terrorism. This is the first order of the day if we are going to salvage the peace process," he told the International Policy Institute for Counterterrorism, which groups former intelligence officials from all over the world.

Ross will arrive in Morocco on Wednesday, the U.S. embassy said in Rabat. Palestinian officials said Arafat was expected to arrive in the Moroccan capital from Bangladesh at around 0400 GMT on Thursday. Netanyahu's office said the prime minister would meet Ross in Jerusalem late on Thursday or on Friday.
A U.S. embassy spokesman in Rabat said Ross would report back to Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright before the weekend.

"We hope that Mr Ross will be speaking loudly and clearly to Mr Netanyahu to stop the causes that led to violence -- to stop his bulldozers, to stop his settlements and to put the peace process back on track," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said.

Israeli political analysts said Ross faced a tall order as he did last year when -- after a wave of violence claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis -- he mediated Israel's handover of most of Hebron to self-rule.
"Ross is going to have to find a formula, like he has before," said Leslie Susser, senior writer of The Jerusalem Report magazine.

"It must be along the lines of the Palestinians making a very strong commitment to crack down on terror and the Israelis committing not to make any more unilateral moves on the peace front," Susser told Reuters.
Palestinians deny charges by Netanyahu that Arafat has given Islamic militants a tacit "green light" to carry out attacks.

Netanyahu repeated the allegation in his speech on Wednesday and said the Palestinian Authority had in the past six months released 150 "terrorist leaders", including 25 of the top leaders of the military arm of the Islamic group Hamas.

"We had warned that the Palestinian terror organisations had received a green light in four successive conversations (with) Palestinian Authority leaders...They emerged with the understanding that they had a green light," he said, without disclosing who Israel had warned.
